analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $17 and eliminates lower wages for tipped and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17, backed by 172 House Democrats, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $9.50 on enactment, then step it up to $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and finally $17 an hour over five years, after which it would rise automatically with the growth in the typical worker's hourly wage [S2]. It would also phase out the separate lower minimum wage for tipped workers, the lower "training" wage for teenagers, and the program that lets employers pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage [S2]. It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, whose pay would rise in scheduled steps to $17 an hour and then keep pace with median wages [S2]. Tipped workers, who are now guaranteed as little as $2.13 an hour in cash wages, would be moved to the full minimum wage over six years [S2]. Workers with disabilities now paid under special subminimum-wage certificates would see their required wage climb to the full minimum within five years [S2]. Newly hired teenagers would also see their lower starting wage raised and eventually eliminated [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 in scheduled steps — $9.50, $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, then $17 — and after five years automatically adjusts it each year by the growth in the median hourly wage of all employees, so the floor no longer erodes for decades as it did between 2009 and 2023 [S2].

Phases out the separate tipped minimum wage, which can be as low as $2.13 an hour, raising the required cash wage for tipped employees over six years until it equals the full minimum wage, and confirms that employees have the right to keep their tips [S2].

Ends the program under which employers hold special certificates to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage: their required wage would rise to $5.00, $7.50, $10.00, $12.50, $15.50, and then the full minimum within five years, no new certificates could be issued, and the authority would sunset, with the Labor Department directed to provide transition assistance and referrals to competitive integrated employment [S2].

Raises the subminimum 'opportunity wage' for newly hired workers under 20 from $4.25 to $6.00 and steps it up each year until it reaches the full minimum wage, at which point the youth subminimum is repealed entirely [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers — restaurants and other food service, retail, hospitality, and the operators of sheltered workshops for workers with disabilities — would bear higher direct wage bills, with the tipped-wage phase-in hitting table-service restaurants hardest [S2]. Some of that cost would be passed to customers through prices, and the Labor Department would spend modest amounts administering the annual median-wage adjustment and transition assistance [S2].

drawbacks.text: The scheduled increases would raise labor costs substantially for low-wage employers, and the steepest burden falls on table-service restaurants, which would have to pay servers the full minimum wage in cash on top of tips; some businesses could respond with higher prices, reduced hours, or fewer staff [S2].

Eliminating the disability subminimum-wage program ends an arrangement some families and sheltered-employment providers argue preserves work opportunities for people with severe disabilities; the bill tries to soften this with a five-year phase-in, a ban only on new certificates, and required Labor Department transition assistance and referrals, but providers would still lose the subminimum model outright [S2].

A higher national floor applies uniformly across states with very different wage levels and living costs, so the same $17 requirement binds employers in low-wage regions more tightly than those in high-wage cities [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are direct and large: the federal minimum had been stuck at $7.25 since 2009, tipped workers could legally be paid $2.13 an hour in cash, and a subset of disabled workers could be paid less than the minimum — all of which this bill would end on fixed schedules [S2]. The costs fall on identifiable businesses, mainly restaurants and other low-wage employers, in the form of higher payrolls and possibly higher prices or reduced hiring. The bill's phased schedule and automatic index to median wage growth are designed to make the increases predictable rather than sudden, which addresses the main economic objection in a standard way; the most debatable design choice is the full abolition of the disability certificate program, which the bill mitigates with a long transition but does not make optional. On balance it is a straightforward transfer from low-wage employers (and their customers) to low-wage workers, drafted with the usual phase-ins.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in July 2023, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia introduced the Raise the Wage Act of 2023 on July 25, 2023, with an initial list of more than 140 Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S2][S4].
The bill attracted 172 cosponsors by the end, every one of them a Democrat; no Republican signed on [S3].
After the referral, the action record shows nothing: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 118th Congress [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it, leaving the federal minimum wage at $7.25 an hour and the tipped cash minimum at $2.13 [S2][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay at or near the federal minimum — restaurant chains, retailers, and operators of sheltered workshops holding disability subminimum certificates — are better off, because the wage floor stays at $7.25 and the tipped and disability subminimum wages remain in place. The bill's sponsors and the millions of workers who would have received raises gained nothing from the outcome.

for.name: Rep. Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott
for.role: Sponsor; senior Democrat on the Education and Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized the initial cosponsor list

for.name: 172 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including leaders such as Nancy Pelosi and Steny Hoyer; no Republican joined

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee agendas in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Brought no minimum wage increase to the House floor during the 118th Congress, and no Republican cosponsored this one

sides.party_line_note: All 172 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-led committee never acted on it [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill phases out the $2.13 tipped cash wage so servers must be paid the full minimum by their employer, directly raising payroll costs for table-service restaurants. Because these businesses profit from the current tipped minimum, their interest in this bill runs against the workers it would raise [S2].

industries.industry: Retail, hospitality, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Any employer paying between $7.25 and $17 an hour would face scheduled raises over five years, then automatic increases tied to median wage growth. These industries' savings from the frozen federal floor come at the expense of the workers it covers [S2].

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and disability subminimum-certificate holders
industries.note: Roughly a hundred thousand workers with disabilities are paid under special 14(c) certificates at wages below the minimum; the bill raises their required wage each year, bans new certificates, and sunsets the program within five years. These employers' business model depends on paying subminimum wages, which is exactly what the bill would end [S2].
